turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. Um, well, honestly... what finally made me come in, what really pushed me to make the appointment, is kind of this specific issue I've been having at work. 

I'm an advertising sales agent—which is a good job, you know, I really like the client interaction part of it—but we have these incredibly long sales strategy meetings. I mean, sometimes they just drag on for hours and hours when we're going over quarterly goals or planning out a huge new campaign. And the thing is... I just keep getting up during them. 

I know I’m supposed to stay seated. Like, everyone else is just sitting there at the conference table, looking at the screen or taking notes, but I just... I can't seem to do it. I'll find any excuse to stand up, even if it’s just to refill my water bottle for the third or fourth time, or I'll go over and just sort of pace by the printer like I'm waiting for a document to come out, even when I'm not printing anything. It’s just, I know it probably looks so unprofessional, and I always tell myself before I walk into the room that I'm going to just sit through the whole thing this time. But then thirty, forty minutes in, I'm already out of my seat again. It's just really starting to get to me, because I feel like my manager and my coworkers are noticing, and I just don't understand why I can't just stay put in my chair like a normal person.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they repeatedly leave their seat during long meetings where they are expected to remain seated, finding excuses to stand up and pace.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school, did you struggle to stay seated or feel this same need to move around during class?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, absolutely. I mean, if I really think about it, this isn't just a recent thing at all. It started way, way before high school. I remember being in elementary school, and it was always a whole production. Like, my parents would go to parent-teacher conferences, and it was always the exact same story every single year. 

My elementary school teachers would always write these long notes on my report cards saying that I was a really bright kid, which was nice, I guess, but there was always a catch. They always wrote that I was bright but I rushed through all my work. Like I couldn't just take my time and sit with it. And the talking, oh my gosh, they constantly said I talked out of turn. I just couldn't hold the thought in, I'd just blurt things out while the teacher was still in the middle of a sentence. 

And it wasn't just the moving around or the talking, either, it was just... everything. I was always forgetting my homework, or I'd actually do it and just lose it somewhere between my kitchen table and the classroom. If you looked inside my desk—you know those little wooden cubby desks where you lift the top up?—mine was just an absolute disaster zone. It was completely stuffed to the brim with all these half-finished papers and crumpled up worksheets. I'd start an assignment, get distracted, shove it in there, and then just never finish it. So, yeah, it's been going on for a really, really long time, this whole chaotic feeling.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions having half-finished papers and starting assignments but never finishing them.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their school desk as an 'absolute disaster zone' stuffed with crumpled papers, indicating difficulty organizing.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient states they would often lose their homework between the kitchen table and the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly notes they would 'get distracted' when trying to do assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions they were 'always forgetting my homework'.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient answers 'Oh, absolutely' to the doctor's question about struggling to stay seated in class.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about the need to move around, referring to 'the moving around' and a 'chaotic feeling'.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient notes that teachers constantly said they 'talked out of turn' and mentions 'the talking'.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient describes blurting things out while the teacher was still in the middle of a sentence.
